Assistant: Of course. There are two main kinds of GPS systems:  coordinate-and- velocity-model (CVM) and  continuous-  Global-Positioning-Sensor (GPS).

Coordinate-and-velocity-model systems use a set of known GPS positions and their corresponding velocities to estimate the  three-dimensional (3D) positions of a satellite and its attached 6- or 12-orbit constellation.  CVM  techniques are widely used in military and other applications where precise 3D positioning is required. These systems cannot be relied upon to accurately track 3D positions of any constellation in the entire world.

Continuous-Global-Positioning-Sensor systems use an array of GPS satellites to measure the time of arrival (TOA) of their signals.  The precise locations of these satellites and the  time of arrival information are combined to measure the precise 3D positions of a receiver. Cutoff-and-Update (CU) techniques correct for the effects of  atmospheric and  ground  reflections between the GPS satellites and the receiver.  These techniques are widely used in the civilian aviation industry and other applications where precise 3D position is required.
